claims.text: TypeSafe AI opened early access to Jev, their SystemOne model, in the week before this post (September 2026).
GeoDeploy pairs TypeSafe Jev with the Pulumi Automation API to place and scale Kubernetes across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud.
GeoDeploy is an open source example available at github.com/pulumi/devx-geodeploy.
TypeSafe's Jev provides AI primitives that let apps, agents, and workflows make decisions based on context.
Jev's decision-making primitives are confidence scoring, multiple choice, and yes/no (noul) questions.

A GeoDeploy deployment request has four parts: target geos (traffic share and data-residency rule of EU-only, US-only, or in-country), an image with platforms (amd64, arm64, or both), a workload shape (replicas, CPU and memory per pod, egress, storage), and constraints (allowed providers, provider count, budget).
GeoDeploy compares every AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud region that offers managed Kubernetes and provisions consistent environments across all three.

In GeoDeploy, the TypeScript app takes the request, fetches pricing and does math; Jev decides region and modules and never does arithmetic, generates code, or invents region names; Pulumi provisions clusters, registries, workloads, and DNS.
GeoDeploy uses great-circle distance as a coverage measure.
GeoDeploy fetches prices from the AWS Price List API, the Azure Retail Prices API, and the Google Cloud Billing Catalog.
GeoDeploy's deterministic TypeScript bin-packs pods onto nodes, filters instance types by image architecture, and computes monthly cost per candidate.
GeoDeploy composes Pulumi programs from typed modules: EKS, AKS, or GKE; ECR, ACR, or Artifact Registry; ingress; DNS via Route 53, NS1, or Cloudflare; and observability.
The Pulumi Automation API runs a preview and then an update with one stack per region, and GeoDeploy won't run unless cloud credentials pass readiness checks.
Every GeoDeploy run writes plan.json and plan.md, and a web UI shows the deployment on a live globe.

Jev provides three primitives: choice() returns the pick, a probability distribution over all options, and a confidence; score() rates against a rubric (GeoDeploy uses 10 levels); noul() answers a yes/no question with a single probability.
Because Jev only selects from closed sets and never writes code or does arithmetic, a hallucinated region or made-up Pulumi argument can't happen by construction.

For each geo, GeoDeploy sends Jev a shortlist of up to 40 priced candidates and in a single call asks for a selection, five quality scores, two hard checks (residency and capacity), and a fallback region.
The @typesafe-ai/sdk package exports choice, noul, and score.
TypeSafe's advice for rubrics is to "describe situations, not degrees."
TypeSafeClient has a systemOne method taking state and questions and returning answers with selection.choice, confidence, residencyOk.noul, and coverage.score.
GeoDeploy's ranking uses weight profiles: latency-optimized (default), balanced, residency-first, and failure-domain, with specified weights.
In GeoDeploy, cluster and registry modules follow from the provider (AWS means EKS and ECR), leaving Jev to decide ingress posture, autoscaling posture, and node-pool sizing tier.

GeoDeploy confidence thresholds: data residency 0.95 (hard reject); new cluster region 0.90 (top three flagged for human); existing stack region 0.75 (keep existing); ingress/autoscaling module 0.85 (registry default); node-pool sizing 0.60 (bin-packing result); global floor 0.50 (drop AI path for that geo).
The residency check is in packages/decide/src/engine.ts in GeoDeploy.
The question definitions are in packages/decide/src/questions.ts in GeoDeploy.
Each AiPathAborted carries the full attempt (state, questions, answers), so rejected answers end up in the audit trail.
If a gate fails, the API times out or errors, or upstream is unreachable, GeoDeploy falls back to a deterministic price comparison across providers while enforcing residency and constraint checks.
The `geodeploy explain` command shows why each region won.

In self-driving mode (`geodeploy monitor`), the agent periodically checks CPU utilization and asks Jev one joint question with options no-change, scale-up:<geo>, scale-down:<geo>, or shift:<from>-><to>, plus a disruption-risk check; code computes node-count changes.

In self-driving mode, above 0.85 confidence the resize is applied automatically, between 0.70 and 0.85 it is suggested for human approval, and below 0.70 GeoDeploy falls back to a deterministic per-region utilization rule.
CPU utilization alone is a poor autoscaling metric and is usually paired with signals like median request latency or error rates.
The Pulumi Automation API page is at /automation/.
In the past, having more choices usually meant more complexity and technical debt.
